uncertainty_note: Applies mainly where aggregation granularity is high enough to support meaningful inference.

title: Analytics disclosures may identify individuals in small aggregates
description: If the backend shares aggregates for small populations, rare events, or narrowly filtered segments, the advertising/analytics partner may be able to single out or recognize an individual behind a metric, especially by combining the disclosure with auxiliary information it already possesses.
assumptions: Assumes some reports include low-count cells, rare conversions, sparse geographies, or other small cohorts.
uncertainty_note: This threat depends strongly on whether minimum-thresholding, suppression, or noise is applied before sharing.

title: Partner may process shared analytics beyond the original app purpose
description: The advertising/analytics partner may use the received analytics not only to provide analytics services or fund the free tier, but also for ad targeting, profiling, model training, cross-client benchmarking, or onward sharing. Such secondary use creates a detectability/disclosure risk because information about app-user behavior becomes exposed to an external party for broader purposes.
assumptions: Assumes contractual or technical controls do not strictly limit partner-side use, retention, and onward disclosure.
uncertainty_note: Detailed classification between disclosure and policy non-compliance can vary by modeling convention; here the concrete privacy harm is exposure of behavioral analytics to the external recipient and possible onward use.

title: Users may be unaware that backend analytics are shared with an advertising/analytics partner
description: Because the sharing occurs server-side, users may not realize their usage and engagement data contributes to disclosures to an external advertising/analytics partner. This reduces transparency about who receives data and for what purpose.
assumptions: Assumes the app's notices are incomplete, vague, or not presented at the relevant time.
uncertainty_note: This is a common risk for backend-to-partner sharing, but actual applicability depends on the quality of privacy notices and in-product explanations.

title: Sharing analytics for monetization may exceed consent or stated privacy commitments
description: Using backend analytics to fund the app's free tier through an advertising/analytics partner may be incompatible with user consent choices, legitimate-purpose limitations, or statements that analytics are only used for service improvement. If the partner receives data for advertising-related monetization without an appropriate legal basis or honoring opt-outs, the flow creates non-compliance risk.
assumptions: Assumes applicable law, platform rules, or the app's own privacy commitments require consent, opt-out honoring, purpose limitation, or data minimization for this type of partner sharing.
uncertainty_note: Legal applicability depends on jurisdiction, exact data fields, whether data is truly anonymous, and the implemented consent/opt-out controls.

title: Child identity can be inferred from the check-in/SOS message
description: The manual check-in/SOS message is sent from the child's account/device to the backend together with current location. Even if the payload were minimized, account identifiers, device identifiers, session tokens, or stable routing metadata can allow the backend or intermediaries to identify which child sent the message.
assumptions: The flow carries or is associated with an authenticated session, device identifier, account identifier, or other stable metadata needed to route the SOS to the correct parent.

title: Repeated SOS/check-in submissions can link the child's activities over time
description: Multiple manual check-ins or SOS messages from the same child can be linked together by the backend using persistent account, device, or network metadata. This enables construction of a longitudinal record of the child's movements and distress events.
assumptions: The backend stores repeated events under the same child or device context.

title: The flow discloses precise real-time location and emergency context
description: The message explicitly contains the child's current location and indicates a manual check-in or SOS event. This reveals highly sensitive personal data, including whereabouts and potentially that the child feels unsafe or needs assistance.
assumptions: Location is sufficiently precise to reveal current whereabouts, and the SOS/check-in semantic is visible to the backend or any party with access to the message.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include the detectability/disclosure subtree.

title: Presence of an SOS/check-in transmission reveals the child's activity or situation
description: Even observing that this flow occurred, without full payload access, may reveal that the child is active at a specific time and may be in a situation requiring attention. Traffic timing, message type, size, or endpoint usage can expose sensitive behavioral information.
assumptions: An observer, service operator, or internal component can see message timing, frequency, or type metadata.

title: Backend-held message records create attributable evidence of the child's actions
description: If the backend stores the submitted SOS/check-in together with account, device, timestamp, and location data, the resulting record can later be used as evidence that the child sent the message from a particular place and time. This reduces the child's ability to plausibly deny having initiated the communication.
assumptions: The backend logs or persists the message with identifiers and timestamps.

title: Collection of child location and SOS data may exceed necessity or valid consent basis
description: Sending precise location and emergency-status information from a child to the backend creates a risk that the system collects or processes more personal data than is necessary for the immediate purpose, or does so without an appropriate legal basis, parental authorization, child assent, retention limit, or transparency notice.
assumptions: The service stores, reuses, or further processes the received location/SOS data beyond transient delivery, or governance around child-data consent and transparency may be incomplete.
